Aquatic Park Bathhouse, San Francisco

A WPA bathhouse of 1936–39 on San Francisco Bay, built like a white ocean liner with rounded decks, ship railings, and portholes.

Source
Library of Congress: HABS CAL,38-SANFRA,157, Aquatic Park Bathhouse
Creator
William Mooser II and William Mooser III, architects; Works Progress Administration
Made
1936–1939 (completed January 1939)
Style
Streamline Moderne (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Nautical, streamlined, civic
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected two Historic American Buildings Survey photographs through their Commons copies at 1920 px: general view, front and side and front elevation. The cars in the photographs date them to about the 1980s. The Library of Congress API returned HTTP 429 (rate limit), so the facts come from Wikipedia and Living New Deal.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Open license, stored. License: public domain. Rights policy

Context

Designed by William Mooser II and III, begun in 1936 and completed in January 1939 as a WPA project, with murals by Hilaire Hiler. Wikipedia: Aquatic Park Historic District; Living New Deal.

The district became a National Historic Landmark District in 1987. The building now houses the San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park’s Maritime Museum. Wikipedia.

Observed

  • The two-storey white block has a fully rounded end; a curved wall of large glass panes wraps the ground-floor corner.
  • Upper decks step back like a ship’s superstructure; each deck has a rounded end and a pipe railing of three horizontal rails.
  • Four round portholes with thick frames line the ground-floor wall; smaller portholes flank the entrance.
  • Groups of three short horizontal grooves (speed lines) sit beside the windows and on the upper wall.
  • Ship details on the roof: ventilator cowls, masts, a flagpole, and an oval name board shaped like a ship’s transom reading “MARITIME MUSEUM”.
  • The walls are smooth and unornamented; the only relief is on the dark stone entrance surround.

Why it belongs

The building shows almost the whole rubric at once: horizontal decks, rounded ends, railings as parallel lines, and portholes, all on a white ground. The ship metaphor is literal because the building faces the bay.

Borrow

Stack horizontal bands that each end in a semicircle, and run three thin parallel rules along the top edge of each band, like a railing.

Use groups of three short horizontal rules beside an element as a speed-line mark.
